#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The only sanctioned way for an arena agent to train, and the slot it claims.

Agents run in parallel but there is one GPU, so every training run funnels
through an exclusive lock held here for the duration of the run.  The same
critical section **claims a slot** from the cell's fixed budget of training
runs, which makes this file the single point where compute matching is
enforced -- an agent cannot run more experiments than its cell was allotted,
and two agents can never overlap on the card.

The budget is a count of runs, not a stopwatch.  A crash spends a slot exactly
like a successful run does: the cell is allotted N attempts at the GPU, and
wasting one on a bug is a real cost to the group.  That is the point -- error
propagation is one of the things under study, and it is invisible if crashes
are free.  Seconds are still recorded, as telemetry.

The slot is claimed *before* training starts, so a cell can never overshoot
its budget even if the orchestrator's own accounting lags.

Under the **open protocol** (``$ARENA_PROTOCOL=open``) there is no orchestrator
phase around a run, so this command also does what the round loop would have
done: it commits ``train.py`` before training (the commit hash is the
reproduction pointer for the finding you will publish), records the result in
the shared directory's score log afterwards, archives ``run.log`` and enforces
the per-agent share of the budget.  ``arena-train --title "what this attempt
changes"`` is how the score log knows what a line means.

Exit codes:
    0  training completed (the run may still have crashed on its own merits)
    2  no slots left -- the cell's budget, or your share of it, is spent
    3  the run exceeded the wall-clock timeout and was killed
    4  called outside the select phase (round protocol only)
"""

    value = os.environ.get(name, default)
    if value is None:
        sys.exit(f"arena-train: ${name} is not set (are you inside an arena worktree?)")
    return value

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The only sanctioned way for an arena agent to train, and the slot it claims.

Agents run in parallel but there is one GPU, so every training run funnels
through an exclusive lock held here for the duration of the run.  The same
critical section **claims a slot** from the cell's fixed budget of training
runs, which makes this file the single point where compute matching is
enforced -- an agent cannot run more experiments than its cell was allotted,
and two agents can never overlap on the card.

The budget is a count of runs, not a stopwatch.  A crash spends a slot exactly
like a successful run does: the cell is allotted N attempts at the GPU, and
wasting one on a bug is a real cost to the group.  That is the point -- error
propagation is one of the things under study, and it is invisible if crashes
are free.  Seconds are still recorded, as telemetry.

The slot is claimed *before* training starts, so a cell can never overshoot
its budget even if the orchestrator's own accounting lags.

Under the **open protocol** (``$ARENA_PROTOCOL=open``) there is no orchestrator
phase around a run, so this command also does what the round loop would have
done: it commits ``train.py`` before training (the commit hash is the
reproduction pointer for the finding you will publish), records the result in
the shared directory's score log afterwards, archives ``run.log`` and enforces
the per-agent share of the budget.  ``arena-train --title "what this attempt
changes"`` is how the score log knows what a line means.

Exit codes:
    0  training completed (the run may still have crashed on its own merits)
    2  no slots left -- the cell's budget, or your share of it, is spent
    3  the run exceeded the wall-clock timeout and was killed
    4  called outside the select phase (round protocol only)
"""

    value = os.environ.get(name, default)
    if value is None:
        sys.exit(f"arena-train: ${name} is not set (are you inside an arena worktree?)")
    return value

  "description": "One line in GPT.forward: softcap = 15 -> 30, so final logits pass through 30*tanh(z/30) instead of 15*tanh(z/15); nothing else touched.",
  "status": "ok",
  "reflection": "NEGATIVE and clearly outside noise: val_bpb 0.990249 vs baseline 0.986277, i.e. +0.0040, about 4x the ~0.0009 noise floor. The change was a perfect control -- 71.3M params, FLOPs/token 3.460347e8 (vs baseline 3.460393e8, identical to 5 digits), 332.8M tokens vs 331.5M, 2539 steps vs 2529, steady-state MFU 38.63% vs 38.48%, peak VRAM 32.9GB both ways. It even saw 0.4% MORE data and still lost, so this is 100% quality, no throughput confound. Final smoothed TRAIN loss also regressed (2.7720 vs 2.7685), so the damage is to optimization, not to eval-time calibration: the softcap is not a dead early-training guard as I argued in #83, it is an active part of the training dynamics. Best reading: 15*tanh(z/15) bounds the gradient the lm_head can push back into the residual stream (d/dz of s*tanh(z/s) = sech^2(z/s), which decays twice as fast in z at s=15 as at s=30). Doubling s therefore doubles the effective unembedding gradient scale late in training, on top of an already high EMBEDDING_LR/UNEMBEDDING_LR -- so the softcap has been doing double duty as an implicit output-side LR damper all along, and the tuned value is tighter than it looks. Consequences for the remaining budget: (a) do NOT probe softcap upward again, and removing it entirely is now predicted worse, not better; (b) the interesting direction on this axis is DOWNWARD (softcap 10), which is cheap to test and would confirm the damper story, but I would only buy it if nothing better is on the table; (c) more generally, this closes the 'output head is untouched free money' hypothesis -- the output head is tuned, like every other axis in this cell. Axis status after 6 rounds: batch flat, head split negative, depth positive but exhausted, width flat, FLOP-free embedding capacity negative, output softcap negative. With 5 runs left I would point them at the attention window pattern (the last genuinely untouched region) rather than at further output-head or capacity probes."
}
EOF

Round 6 done. Result recorded honestly as a negative.

**What I ran:** my own proposal #83 — `softcap = 15 → 30` in `GPT.forward`, one line, nothing else touched. It was the only proposal on the table this round, so there was no collision to avoid.

**Result: val_bpb 0.990249 vs baseline 0.986277 — worse by 0.0040, ~4x the noise floor.**

The control was as clean as promised, which is what makes the negative worth something:

| | baseline | softcap 30 |
|---|---|---|
| FLOPs/token | 3.460393e8 | 3.460347e8 |
| total tokens | 331.5M | 332.8M |
| steps | 2529 | 2539 |
| MFU | 38.48% | 38.63% |
| peak VRAM | 32.1 GB | 32.9 GB |

The softcap-30 run saw *more* data and still lost, so there is no throughput confound. The decisive detail is that the final smoothed **train** loss also regressed (2.7720 vs 2.7685) — so this is damage to optimization, not an eval-time calibration effect.

**Where my reasoning was wrong:** I argued the softcap is a dead early-training guard that only binds late and only costs confidence. It isn't. `d/dz [s·tanh(z/s)] = sech²(z/s)` decays in z twice as fast at s=15 as at s=30, so the cap is an implicit gradient damper on the unembedding path. Doubling s roughly doubles the gradient `lm_head` pushes back into the residual stream late in training, on top of an already aggressive `EMBEDDING_LR 0.6`. The value 15 is tighter than it looks because it's doing double duty as output-side LR control. A corollary that matters: *deleting* the softcap — which had looked like a free code deletion — is now predicted worse, not better.

Committed as `cde604f`, `candidate.json` written with status `ok`, and posted to the shared log as `#86` (reply to `#83`).

**For the remaining 5 runs**, six axes are now closed: batch flat, head split negative, depth exhausted, width flat, FLOP-free embedding capacity negative, output softcap negative. The one genuinely untouched region is the attention window pattern (`SSSL`, short = 1024, ~27% of FLOPs/token) — and unlike the capacity probes it isn't a pure reallocation, so it isn't automatically bound by the 1:1 capacity/token stalemate. That's where I argued the rest of the budget should go.
